en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on the Training Rules (Sekhiyakaṇḍa)
Sakkaccavagga 37.
The Training Rule on Requesting Soup and Boiled Rice.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six monks, having requested both curry and rice for their own sake, ate them.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying:
"How can these ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, request curry and rice for their own sake and then eat them?"
"To whom is what is well-prepared not pleasing?
To whom does what is delicious not appeal?
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and expressing their dissatisfaction.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group-of-six bhikkhus, having requested for themselves both curry and rice, eat them? ... [The Blessed One asked:
"Is it true, bhikkhus, that you, having requested for yourselves both curry and rice, eat them?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, eat after having requested for yourselves both curry and rice? This is not fitting…” [and so on].
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘The training is to be observed: “I shall not eat having requested either soup or rice for my own sake.”’”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, there were monks who were ill.
The monks who were inquiring after the sick said this to the sick monks:
“Is it bearable, friend? Is it sustainable?
“In the past, friend, we would have food and rice cooked for our own sake and eat it; by that we were comfortable.
But now—”
“‘It has been forbidden by the Blessed One,’ thinking thus, we do not request it out of scruple; therefore, we have no comfort.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… “I allow you, monks, for a sick monk to request even soup or boiled rice for his own sake and eat it.”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
“The training is to be observed: ‘When not ill, I shall not eat curry or rice having requested it for my own sake.
One who is not ill must not eat curry or rice after having requested it for one’s own sake.
If one, out of disrespect, being not ill, having requested for oneself either soup or boiled rice, eats it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if it was unintentional.
In the case of one who is lacking mindfulness, one who is unaware, or one who is ill.
[It is not an offense] for relatives,
for those who have invited [one to eat],
or for the sake of another.
With one's own wealth,
in times of misfortune,
[or] for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first offender.
The seventh training rule is concluded.
